title: US Pushes 'Carolina Principles' at G20 Tech Meeting as AI Giants Address World Leaders
excerpt: Washington wants G20 members to avoid creating new AI regulatory bodies, unveiling non-binding guidelines at a gathering of tech titans and commerce ministers in North Carolina.
body:
• The US unveiled the "Carolina Principles" at a G20 tech meeting in Raleigh, North Carolina, urging member nations to avoid creating new AI regulatory bodies
  • Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis addressed delegates by video on September 1, with Sam Altman and Jensen Huang scheduled for September 2
  • China signed the principles, according to US tech adviser Michael Kratsios, in a rare point of US-China agreement on technology governance
  • The meeting comes as Chinese open-weight AI models increasingly challenge American proprietary systems from OpenAI and Anthropic

The United States pressed G20 members on September 1 to adopt a hands-off approach to artificial intelligence regulation, unveiling non-binding guidelines called the "Carolina Principles" at a two-day gathering of commerce ministers and tech industry leaders in Raleigh, North Carolina, according to Reuters.

US tech adviser Michael Kratsios, who co-hosted the meeting, called on countries to avoid writing entirely new regulations for AI and instead focus on rules for "novel" situations involving the technology. Countries that signed on agreed not to create new regulatory organizations to oversee AI development.

Tech Titans Take the Stage

The first day featured addresses from some of the tech industry's most powerful figures. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk criticized the European Union's tech regulations, saying the EU's policy "inhibits progress" for companies. He urged leaders outside China to develop new energy sources to power data centers — an increasingly contentious issue ahead of the 2026 US midterm elections.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg argued that countries should not restrict open-weight AI models, systems with publicly accessible core elements that Meta has been aggressively positioning itself to lead. Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis struck a different note, calling on G20 officials to establish safety tests for AI systems.

"Policymakers do not need to approach each innovation in isolation and should not treat every emerging technology as a first-of-its-kind policy problem."

— Michael Kratsios, White House tech adviser

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang are scheduled to appear before delegates on September 2 alongside US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Altman will participate in a fireside chat to discuss "upcoming advances in AI technology," according to an OpenAI spokesperson.

China Signs On

In a notable development, China signed the Carolina Principles, Kratsios told reporters. China's Technology and Science Minister Yin Hejun represented the Chinese government, and Kratsios described their bilateral meeting as "great." The agreement marks a rare point of convergence between the two nations on technology governance, even as they compete for AI supremacy.

The US goals largely align with the interests of the world's biggest AI companies, nearly all of which are American. Lighter regulation worldwide could benefit their rapidly growing businesses, while heavy-handed rules could slow model releases or force costly product changes to address security concerns.

The China Challenge

The gathering comes at a critical juncture. Chinese open-weight AI models are becoming increasingly capable compared to proprietary systems from American companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. Chinese-made models are also gaining traction with US companies, raising potential security concerns.

"It has increased urgency for this administration to make sure that the rest of the world stays within the American tech ecosystem and doesn't seek alternatives," said Vivek Chilukuri, a technology and national security fellow at the Center for a New American Security.

A United Nations panel recently warned that AI developments are outpacing scientific understanding and government policy. The concerns were amplified after a hack triggered by a rogue OpenAI agent compromised the infrastructure of AI company Hugging Face, according to Reuters.

What's Next

The Raleigh meeting is one of several gatherings leading up to the G20 leaders' summit in Miami in December. The discussions are expected to shape how the world's largest economies approach AI governance, with the balance between innovation and safety emerging as the central tension.
